nodes.label: County Court: jurisdiction over civil claims (contract, tort, equity, up to unlimited value subject to allocation)
High Court: jurisdiction and three divisions (Queen's/King's Bench, Chancery, Family)
Pre-trial procedure: issuing a claim, particulars of claim, defence, case management by courts
Woolf reforms and the Civil Procedure Rules 1998: overriding objective of dealing with cases justly and at proportionate cost
Small claims track: claims up to £10,000, informal procedure
Fast track: claims £10,000-£25,000, fixed procedure with limited disclosure
Multi-track: claims over £25,000, case managed individually by judge
Track allocation: court allocates case to a track based on value, complexity and other factors
Civil appeal routes: from County Court/High Court to Court of Appeal (Civil Division) and onward to Supreme Court
Leapfrog appeals: direct appeal from High Court to Supreme Court in limited circumstances
Tribunals: purpose, structure (First-tier and Upper Tribunal), use for specialist statutory disputes
Negotiation: parties or their representatives settle a dispute directly without a third party
Mediation: neutral third party facilitates agreement, non-binding, parties control outcome
Conciliation: neutral third party actively suggests solutions to help parties reach agreement
Arbitration: parties agree to submit dispute to a neutral arbitrator whose decision (award) is binding, governed by Arbitration Act 1996
Online courts and Online Dispute Resolution: use of technology (e.g. Money Claim Online, HMCTS reform programme) to resolve disputes without physical hearings
Evaluation: cost of civil litigation as a barrier compared to ADR/tribunals
Evaluation: delay in civil courts versus speed of ADR and tribunals
Evaluation: formality and complexity of civil court procedure deterring litigants in person
Evaluation: ADR offers privacy and preserves relationships compared to public adversarial court hearings
Evaluation: mediation/conciliation outcomes are not binding and may lack enforceability compared to court judgments
Evaluation: arbitration can be as costly and slow as litigation despite being marketed as an alternative
Evaluation: tribunals offer cheaper, faster, specialist justice but fees have reduced access (e.g. R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor)
Evaluation: online courts/ODR improve access and efficiency but raise concerns over digital exclusion and lack of open justice
Summary offences: minor offences tried only in the Magistrates' Court
Indictable offences: serious offences tried only in the Crown Court before a jury
Either-way offences: can be tried in either the Magistrates' Court or the Crown Court
Mode of trial procedure for either-way offences: plea before venue and allocation hearing
Magistrates' Court jurisdiction: summary trials, first hearings for all offences, sending indictable/either-way cases to Crown Court
Crown Court jurisdiction: trial on indictment before judge and jury, sentencing powers
Bail: right to bail under Bail Act 1976 and grounds for refusal
Plea and case management: early guilty plea reductions and case management hearings
Appeals from Magistrates' Court: to Crown Court (fact/law/sentence) or by case stated to High Court (Divisional Court) on point of law
Appeals from Crown Court: defence appeal to Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction/sentence; prosecution right to appeal on point of law or unduly lenient sentence
Further appeal from Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) to Supreme Court on point of law of general public importance
Attorney General's reference: referring an unduly lenient sentence or a point of law following acquittal
Criminal Cases Review Commission: reviewing suspected miscarriages of justice and referring cases to Court of Appeal
Sentencing aim: punishment/retribution
Sentencing aim: deterrence (individual and general)
Sentencing aim: reform and rehabilitation
Sentencing aim: public protection/incapacitation
Sentencing aim: reparation to victims or community
Sentencing factor: aggravating factors increasing sentence severity
Sentencing factor: mitigating factors reducing sentence severity
Sentencing Council guidelines: structuring judicial discretion in sentencing
Custodial sentences: fixed-term, life, suspended sentences
Community sentences: requirements such as unpaid work, curfew, rehabilitation activity
Fines: financial penalty as a sentence
Discharges: absolute and conditional discharge
Lay magistrates: qualifications and eligibility criteria (age, residency, character requirements)
Lay magistrates: selection and appointment process via local advisory committees
Lay magistrates: role in criminal cases (summary trials, early hearings, sending cases, youth court)
Jurors: qualifications and eligibility under Juries Act 1974
Jury selection: random selection from electoral roll, vetting and challenges
Jury role: determining verdict on facts in Crown Court trials, majority verdicts
Evaluation: custodial sentences incapacitate but have high reoffending rates and cost
Evaluation: community sentences rehabilitate and are cost-effective but seen as a soft option
Evaluation: fines are flexible and easy to administer but can be unfair given differing means and difficult to enforce
Evaluation: discharges avoid stigmatising minor offenders but provide little deterrence
Evaluation: lay magistrates provide local community input but are criticised as unrepresentative of society
Evaluation: lay magistrates receive free, quick, cost-effective justice but lack of legal training risks inconsistency
Evaluation: reliance on legal advisers/clerks and prosecution bias concerns regarding lay magistrates
Evaluation: jury as representative of the public and a democratic safeguard
Evaluation: jury secrecy prevents scrutiny of reasoning, raising concerns over perverse verdicts (contempt of Court Act 1981 s8)
Evaluation: jurors may struggle to understand complex evidence, e.g. in fraud trials
Evaluation: risk of jury nobbling/intimidation and susceptibility to media influence
Evaluation: jury trials are costly and slow compared to summary trial
Solicitors: qualifications, training routes (including SQE), work and areas of practice
Solicitors: regulation by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA)
Barristers: qualifications, training (academic, vocational, pupillage), work including advocacy
Barristers: regulation by the Bar Standards Board (BSB)
Chartered Legal Executives: qualifications, training and work, regulated by CILEx Regulation
Trends: fusion of roles between solicitors and barristers, e.g. solicitor-advocates
Impact of technology on legal services: online services, AI-assisted document review, virtual hearings
Impact of globalisation on legal services: international law firms, cross-border legal practice
Judiciary: qualifications required for judicial appointment (relevant legal qualification and experience)
Judicial Appointments Commission: role in selection and appointment of judges, replacing the old 'secret soundings' system
Judicial training: role of the Judicial College in ongoing training
Role of the judiciary: presiding over trials, case management, sentencing, developing precedent
Judicial retirement: mandatory retirement age
Judicial removal: security of tenure, removal only for misbehaviour via address to both Houses of Parliament (senior judges) or Lord Chancellor (inferior judges)
Separation of powers doctrine: division between legislature, executive and judiciary (Montesquieu)
Judicial independence: security of tenure, immunity from suit, independence from executive/legislature underpinning the rule of law
Constitutional Reform Act 2005: creation of Supreme Court, JAC and reforms strengthening separation of powers
Evaluation: divided profession (solicitors/barristers) offers specialisation but causes duplication of cost and inefficiency for clients
Evaluation: CILEx route improves access to the legal profession for non-graduates but has narrower rights than solicitors/barristers
Evaluation: technology increases efficiency and access to legal services but risks reducing personal client care and raises cybersecurity concerns
Evaluation: globalisation increases competition and choice but disadvantages smaller domestic firms
Evaluation: JAC improves transparency in appointments but judiciary remains criticised as unrepresentative in diversity
Evaluation: security of tenure and removal safeguards protect judicial independence and impartial decision-making
Evaluation: Lord Chancellor's continuing role and executive influence over appointments/discipline can undermine perceived judicial independence
Origins of state funding: Legal Aid and Advice Act 1949 establishing legal aid
LASPO 2012: Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act reforms restricting scope of civil legal aid
Civil legal aid: means and merits tests, scope limited mainly to specific categories (e.g. family/domestic abuse, housing, asylum)
Criminal legal aid: right to representation, means and interests-of-justice tests, duty solicitor scheme
Legal Aid Agency: administers state funding for legal aid
Private funding: paying privately for legal fees out of own resources
Legal expenses insurance: before-the-event (BTE) insurance covering legal costs
Conditional fee agreements ('no win, no fee'): solicitor's success fee payable only if case is won, funded under Courts and Legal Services Act 1990 as amended
Damages-based agreements: lawyer's fee paid as a percentage of damages recovered
Trade union and other group funding: unions or organisations funding members' legal claims
Pro bono work: free legal services provided voluntarily by lawyers
Citizens Advice Bureau and other advice agencies: free initial advice and signposting
Law centres: free legal services in local communities, often for disadvantaged groups
Evaluation: LASPO cuts saved public money but created advice deserts and reduced access to justice for civil claimants
Evaluation: criminal legal aid safeguards fair trial rights but funding cuts and low fees reduce solicitor availability
Evaluation: CFAs improve access to justice for those without means but success fees/insurance costs can erode damages and deter risk-averse solicitors
Evaluation: private funding provides full choice of representation but creates inequality of access based on wealth
Evaluation: advice agencies and law centres widen access but are underfunded and cannot replace full legal representation
Evaluation: pro bono work helps some litigants but is inconsistent, unpredictable and cannot meet overall demand
